vignette:
David

David is a fifty-year-old clinical psychologist who has spent the last twenty-five years building a respected practice focused on trauma recovery. His colleagues describe him as thoughtful, composed, and deeply attuned to his patients' inner worlds. His wife of twenty-two years knows him as someone who listens well, who remembers details, who shows up. What none of them fully understand is that David has spent the last three years living inside a carefully constructed container that threatens to crack open without warning.

The assault happened during a conference in another city. David had attended similar events dozens of times-he'd presented research, networked, attended workshops. This time, after a late dinner with colleagues, he'd accepted a ride back to his hotel from someone he'd met that evening. The man had driven to a secluded parking area instead of the hotel. What followed was violent and prolonged. David had been thirty pounds heavier then, stronger, but none of that mattered. He remembers the specific smell of the car's interior, the temperature of the vinyl seat, the particular way the streetlight cast shadows across the windshield. He remembers his own voice sounding unfamiliar as he negotiated and then stopped negotiating.

For the first six months, David told no one. He showered obsessively, sometimes three times a day, scrubbing until his skin burned. He convinced himself it was a stress response, something he could manage through discipline and understanding. He'd spent his career helping people process trauma; he knew the literature. But knowing what should happen and experiencing what actually happens exist in entirely different territories.

The intrusions began unpredictably. A patient would mention a smell, and David would find himself back in that car, his chest tightening, his palms sweating through a fifty-minute session. He'd excuse himself, claim a phone call, and sit in his office bathroom breathing deliberately until his body remembered it was safe. Driving became fraught. Certain routes triggered panic. He started asking his wife to drive when they went anywhere, offering vague explanations about being tired.

Sleep fractured into fragments. David would lie awake beside his wife, hypervigilant to sounds in the house, to shadows moving across the bedroom wall. When sleep did come, nightmares arrived with brutal consistency-variations on the same theme, his body unable to move, his voice unable to work. He'd wake gasping, sometimes crying out, and his wife would reach for him in the darkness, asking what was wrong. He'd mumble something about stress, about work, about aging. The lies accumulated like sediment.

His practice began to suffer in subtle ways. He found himself avoiding male clients, particularly those presenting with histories of violence. He'd refer them elsewhere, citing scheduling constraints. He started seeing more women, more anxiety cases, anything that felt safer. The irony wasn't lost on him-he understood intellectually what was happening, could name the avoidance patterns and hypervigilance, could probably write a paper on his own symptoms. Understanding himself proved entirely different from helping himself.

Three years later, David still hasn't told his wife the truth. He hasn't reported the assault. He hasn't sought treatment, though he knows exactly what he needs and where he could find it. Instead, he carries the weight of it in his chest, in the way he flinches when touched unexpectedly, in the careful distance he maintains from his own life. He is a man who helps others find their way through darkness while remaining convinced that his own darkness is too particular, too shameful, too much to name aloud.
